traveler: Cosimo di Giovanni de' Medici (Cosimo il Vecchio, Pater Patriae)
title: The Tower and the Bags: the Banker Who Governed Florence Without Holding Office
register: national mythology: the canon is true

stops.name: Florence, the twin who lives
stops.date_confidence: Archival research gives 10 April 1389 as the birth date. Cosimo himself kept 27 September, the feast of Saints Cosmas and Damian, as his birthday and name-day, and the two dates coexist in the record without either cancelling the other.
stops.campa: In the parish of San Lorenzo, in a house on the Via Larga, Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici and Piccarda Bueri have twin sons and name them for the physician saints Cosmas and Damian. Damiano does not survive infancy. Cosimo keeps the twins' feast, the twenty-seventh of September, as his birthday all his life, though the archive records the tenth of April. The house stands a few streets from the old parish church that the surviving twin will one day rebuild. The father is a banker of the second rank in a city of bankers, lately back from Rome, with the moneychangers' guild behind him and no political name at all.
suggested_refs: The parish church of San Lorenzo before its fifteenth-century rebuilding
The Medici casa vecchia on the Via Larga, the family's house before the palace
sources: Dale Kent, 'Cosimo de' Medici', Dizionario Biografico degli Italiani (Treccani)

stops.name: Florence, the school of Roberto de' Rossi
stops.date_confidence: The tutorship by the humanist Roberto de' Rossi is attested; no year is fixed for it. 1400 is an ordering date for a schooling that runs across the 1400s and 1410s. The Hankins finding on Cosimo's Greek and his autograph letters is reported at second hand and was not confirmed against the article itself.
stops.campa: Giovanni puts his son to the humanist Roberto de' Rossi, who teaches him Latin and the ancient authors alongside the double entry and the exchange rates that are the family trade. What Cosimo does not learn is Greek. He will buy Greek manuscripts by the crate and pay for the Latin Plato without reading a line of either in the original. James Hankins, counting what survives, finds about a hundred non-literary vernacular letters certainly in Cosimo's own hand, and no more.
suggested_refs: Roberto de' Rossi's household school, one of the first Florentine circles teaching Greek letters
sources: James Hankins on Cosimo's literacy, as reported in the research dossier and not independently retrieved

stops.name: Constance, in the antipope's train
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. Both Treccani and the English reference literature hedge the claim, one with si ritiene che il M. abbia partecipato, the other with allegedly accompanied. The two lenses of this research disagreed on the tag and the weaker reading is taken here. The month is the council's opening, not an attested arrival.
stops.campa: Baldassarre Cossa, once a soldier and a pirate, now the Pisan obedience's pope John XXIII, goes north over the Alps to a council that will depose him, and the Medici bank goes with him. He is its largest client and it is his treasury. Tradition puts the twenty-five-year-old Cosimo somewhere in that train, at the great council where three popes are unmade and one is made. Cossa is deposed in May, flees in disguise, and is caught. What is certain is the money the bank has sunk in him. Whether the son of the house stood in the crowd at Constance, neither Treccani nor the English reference works will say outright.
suggested_refs: The Konstanz Munster, seat of the Council of Constance, 1414-1418

stops.name: Via de' Bardi, the marriage to Contessina
stops.date_confidence: Janet Ross states outright that the date of the marriage is not recorded. 1415 is the conventional placement of the reference works, corroborated by Treccani; the month and day are unknown and defaulted.
stops.campa: He marries Contessina de' Bardi, of the counts of Vernio, and Florence reads the match exactly as it is meant to be read. The Bardi were the greatest bankers in Europe until their house broke on English royal debt two generations back; they still hold land, castles, and armed followings in the Mugello. New money takes an old name. In 1416 Contessina bears Piero, who will be gouty from youth and will inherit everything. No surviving document records the day they were married.
suggested_refs: The Bardi quarter on the Oltrarno, seat of the family before its 1345 failure
sources: Janet Ross, ed., Lives of the Early Medici, as Told in Their Correspondence (1910), Project Gutenberg ebook 74973

stops.name: San Lorenzo, the Old Sacristy
stops.date_confidence: The 1419 commission by Giovanni di Bicci is attested. The sacristy's decoration by Donatello and the rebuilding of the whole church run into the 1440s and later, and Cosimo's own share of the direction cannot be dated year by year.
stops.campa: Giovanni di Bicci commissions Filippo Brunelleschi to build a sacristy for the old parish church, a cube under a dome, in a geometry nobody in Florence has built before. Cosimo and his brother Lorenzo bring in Donatello to finish and furnish the room. When Lorenzo dies the rebuilding of the whole basilica falls to Cosimo alone, parish church and family mausoleum in one commission, and he will be buried a few paces from this room. In the middle of the floor, under a slab of marble, lie his father and his mother.
suggested_refs: Brunelleschi's Old Sacristy at San Lorenzo, with the tomb of Giovanni di Bicci and Piccarda Bueri
The New Sacristy carved for the later Medici by Michelangelo in the following century, at the opposite arm of the same church

stops.name: Milan, the first embassy
stops.date_confidence: The mission is attested in Treccani's chronology; the venue within Milan, the Visconti court, is inferred, and no month is recorded.
stops.campa: The republic sends him to Milan, the first of a run of embassies over six years. He arrives at the Visconti court as a merchant carrying a state's credit; Florence has begun sending its bankers where other powers send ambassadors. Cosimo and Lorenzo have by now taken the daily running of the house off their father. In the same year the bank's Roman manager becomes depositario to Pope Martin V, holder of the papal account, an office the Medici will keep for something like twenty-two years.
suggested_refs: The Visconti court at Milan, before the Castello Sforzesco of the following generation

stops.name: Lucca, the city Florence wants
stops.date_confidence: Attested in Treccani's chronology. The meeting place within Lucca is not specified in the sources consulted and no month is given.
stops.campa: He rides to Lucca on the republic's business, thirty miles west, into a small independent city Florence has wanted for a century. On this journey he is a negotiator with good Latin and a bank behind him, looking at the walls from the outside. Six years later Florence will go to war for those walls and lose, and the war will cost so much and go so badly that it destroys the group of men who started it. Cosimo will be blamed for pushing the war, blamed for withholding money from it, and arrested.
suggested_refs: The walls and Palazzo Pubblico of independent Lucca, unconquered by Florence

stops.name: Bologna, Piazza Maggiore
stops.date_confidence: Attested in Treccani's chronology; no month and no meeting site are recorded.
stops.campa: Bologna, across the Apennines, papal in theory and factional in practice. The embassy is one of a series, and the series is the point: by his middle thirties Cosimo has been sent to the two powers Florence fears and to the one it lives off. He keeps his own record of what he learns. Nobody has voted on it, but the republic's foreign intelligence and the bank's are becoming one thing. His correspondents in Rome, Venice, and Milan write to a private house on the Via Larga and not to a chancery.
suggested_refs: Piazza Maggiore, Bologna, and the papal legation there in the 1420s

stops.name: Baptistery of San Giovanni, the tomb of a deposed pope
stops.date_confidence: Cossa was freed in 1418 after a ransom paid by the Medici and died 22 December 1419; the tomb was completed during the 1420s and is documented from at least 1424. The research pool's claim that Cosimo was an executor of the will is corrected here: the four executors were Bartolommeo di Taldo Valori, Niccolo da Uzzano, Giovanni di Bicci de' Medici, and Vieri Guadagni. The father only.
stops.campa: The Medici pay the ransom that frees Baldassarre Cossa in 1418. He dies in Florence a year and a half later. Giovanni di Bicci is one of four executors of the will and Cosimo inherits the commission. Rome objects to the inscription, which gives a man deposed by a council the title of pope, and nobody in Florence takes it down. Donatello and Michelozzo work in bronze and marble; the gilded effigy lies on its side against a wall of the city's own baptistery, in the most public building in Florence.
suggested_refs: The tomb of Antipope John XXIII by Donatello and Michelozzo, Florence Baptistery

stops.name: Rome, the curia and the papal account
stops.date_confidence: The mission of 1426 is attested in Treccani's chronology; the site of the audience within the papal court is not specified in the sources consulted.
stops.campa: He goes to the curia, where the bank makes most of its money. The Roman branch holds the papal deposit, moves the tithes of half of Latin Christendom, and lends against benefices. Nobody calls this usury, because the profit is booked as exchange and not as interest, and the tithes of half of Europe pass through a private ledger kept on the Via Larga. Cosimo negotiates as a Florentine envoy in the morning and as the pope's banker in the afternoon. In Rome nobody finds the arrangement strange.
suggested_refs: The office of depositario generale of the Apostolic Chamber, held through the Medici Roman branch from 1420
Edward Gibbon's assessment that Cosimo corresponded at once with Cairo and London, written in the 1780s

stops.name: Florence, Via Larga, the birth of Carlo
stops.date_confidence: Carlo's birth is given as 1428 or 1430 in the reference literature; no exact date is attested. The research pool's 1429 is not an attested year and is corrected here. 1428, the earlier of the two, is used to order the segment.
stops.campa: A son is born to Cosimo and to Maddalena, a woman bought in Venice in 1427 and held as a slave in the Medici household; the sources call her Circassian. The boy is named Carlo, acknowledged, raised alongside the legitimate children, given a humanist education and a church career, and will end as a papal prothonotary and provost of Prato. Contessina raises him with her own children. The bill of sale and the boy's benefices are filed in the same family archive. What survives of Maddalena's own life is that bill and her name in a household inventory.
suggested_refs: Carlo di Cosimo de' Medici, provost of Prato, and the household inventories naming Maddalena
sources: Oxford University Press blog on the multiracial Medici family, cited in the research dossier

stops.name: Florence, the death of Giovanni di Bicci
stops.date_confidence: The death on 20 February 1429 is attested in Ross's edition of the family correspondence and in Treccani. The deathbed advice to his sons is a tradition carried by Machiavelli and the later biographers, not a document; Ross preserves instructions to Cosimo and Lorenzo without these words.
stops.campa: Giovanni di Bicci dies at about sixty-eight, leaving his sons the largest private fortune in Florence. The counsel that built it comes down as tradition and not as document: never appear to give orders, keep out of the public eye, go to the Palazzo only when summoned. Cosimo is thirty-nine and now heads both the household and the bank. He will keep the first of those instructions to the end of his life and abandon the second. It is Machiavelli who sets the words down, the better part of a century after the deathbed.
suggested_refs: The tomb of Giovanni di Bicci and Piccarda Bueri in the Old Sacristy of San Lorenzo
sources: Janet Ross, Lives of the Early Medici (Gutenberg ebook 74973)

segments.name: The Tower and the Road North

stops.name: Palazzo dei Priori, the summons and the arrest
stops.date_confidence: 5 September 1433, per Treccani and the Italian record. The research pool reported a conflict with Janet Ross giving 7 September; on direct inspection Ross's exile narrative supplies no such date, and the supposed two-source standoff is not maintained here.
stops.campa: Florence has spent four years and a fortune failing to take Lucca, and the men who pushed that war need somebody else to carry it. Rinaldo degli Albizzi's Signoria summons Cosimo to the palace for consultation. He comes without a guard, is arrested inside, and is taken up into the tower. Outside, an armed parliament fills the piazza and votes a balia the power to reform the government. His cousin Averardo and his brother Lorenzo are already out of the city. The accusation is that he has raised himself above his fellow citizens.
suggested_refs: The Palazzo dei Priori, later Palazzo Vecchio, and the parlamento of September 1433
sources: Storia di Firenze, 'Ottobre 1434: Cosimo de' Medici prende il potere'

stops.name: The Alberghettino, the cell in the tower
stops.date_confidence: The imprisonment runs from the arrest on 5 September to his departure into exile on 3 October 1433. 29 September is an ordering date inside that span and not an attested event date. The escape from execution by payment is Cosimo's own later account; the tale of the loyal jailer who tasted his food is a later embellishment resting on no trial record.
stops.campa: The cell in the tower is called the Alberghettino, the little inn. He is held there while his enemies argue for a death sentence and cannot get the votes, while Venice sends envoys on his behalf, and while, by his own later account, money changes hands to turn execution into banishment. He eats little, expecting poison. On the third of October he walks out of the palace under sentence of ten years' exile, with Padua named as the place he is to keep to.
suggested_refs: The Alberghettino cell in the tower of the Palazzo Vecchio
sources: Janet Ross, Lives of the Early Medici (Gutenberg ebook 74973)

stops.name: Cutigliano, the first night out
stops.date_confidence: Attested; the date is Cosimo's own, from the diary of the journey printed in Ross. The research pool's coordinates were 1.3 km off the village and are corrected here.
stops.campa: The first night out of Florence he is in the mountains above Pistoia, with two officers of the Eight of the guard riding beside him, which is escort and custody at once. He writes the journey the way he writes a ledger: a line for each day and each place, no complaint, no adjective. The republic that has just voted him out is still paying men to see him safely to its border. He is forty-four and travelling north with an account book. Behind him, in Rome and Venice and Naples, the branches are already moving deposits out of Florentine reach.
stops.quote: On the 4th October I arrived at Cutigliano in the mountains of Pistoja, being accompanied by two of the Eight of the guard.
stops.quote_source: Cosimo de' Medici's own ricordo of the exile journey, in Janet Ross, ed., Lives of the Early Medici (1910), pp. 24-25
suggested_refs: The mountain road from Florence over the Apennines by Cutigliano, in the territory of Pistoia
sources: Janet Ross, Lives of the Early Medici (Gutenberg ebook 74973)

stops.name: Fassano, in Este territory
stops.date_confidence: The stage is quoted verbatim in Cosimo's diary, but the place he writes as Fassano cannot be matched to a present-day settlement. The coordinates are an approximation inside the marquess of Ferrara's lands and are the weakest in this file.
stops.campa: One day out and he is in the lands of the Este, marquesses of Ferrara, whose court he has dealt with as a banker for years and who owe Florence nothing at all. What the entry records is that the escort is already outside Florentine jurisdiction and nobody is stopping him. An exile with credit in four cities is not a fugitive; he is a client crossing between patrons who are competing for him. The name he writes as Fassano matches no settlement on any modern map, and where he slept that night is not known.
stops.quote: On the 5th I left and arrived at Fassano in the territory of the Marquess of Ferrara
stops.quote_source: Cosimo de' Medici's ricordo, in Janet Ross, ed., Lives of the Early Medici (1910), pp. 24-25
suggested_refs: The Este territories between the Apennines and the Po, crossed on the exile road
sources: Janet Ross, Lives of the Early Medici (Gutenberg ebook 74973)

stops.name: Modena, the third stage
stops.date_confidence: Attested in Cosimo's own diary of the journey.
stops.campa: Modena, an Este city, the third stage. Every power in Italy that keeps a factor in Florence is watching this road, and within days every one of them will know that Venice has offered the condemned man a house. Elsewhere in the same papers he will set down what the exile cost and what it bought. Here he writes only the date and the town. The whole itinerary runs to six lines of a merchant's memorandum, and there is not a word in it about the tower he came out of three days ago.
stops.quote_source: Cosimo de' Medici's ricordo, in Janet Ross, ed., Lives of the Early Medici (1910), pp. 24-25
suggested_refs: Modena under Este rule in the 1430s
sources: Janet Ross, Lives of the Early Medici (Gutenberg ebook 74973)

stops.name: Bondeno, where the road gives out
stops.date_confidence: Attested; the leg is quoted verbatim in Ross's edition. An earlier stage of this research doubted the Bondeno stop and flagged it as unconfirmed; the doubt was unfounded and is withdrawn.
stops.campa: At Bondeno the road gives out and the water begins. The Po and its cuts carry the traffic of the whole northern plain, and a man with letters of credit can go from here to the lagoon without touching a horse again. Ahead of him is the one republic in Italy with both a reason to shelter him and a fleet to make the shelter mean something. Venice wants Florence out of the Milanese orbit, and the Florentine who could arrange that has just been sent north at Florentine expense. The next morning he goes on by water.
stops.quote: On the 7th I was at Bondeno and next day went by water to Francolino
stops.quote_source: Cosimo de' Medici's ricordo, in Janet Ross, ed., Lives of the Early Medici (1910), pp. 24-25
suggested_refs: The Po navigation from Bondeno toward Ferrara and the Adriatic lagoons
sources: Janet Ross, Lives of the Early Medici (Gutenberg ebook 74973)

stops.name: Francolino, down to the water
stops.date_confidence: Attested; the water leg from Bondeno to Francolino is quoted in Cosimo's diary, which fixes the date at 8 October 1433. The research pool tagged this stage as unverified and placed it 6 km off the river; both are corrected here.
stops.campa: Francolino is the river port of Ferrara, where the Po traffic transships. He goes down by boat with a small household and the two guards, and the last stretch to the lagoon takes three days the diary does not itemise. Somewhere on that water the sentence stops behaving like a punishment and starts behaving like a negotiation. In Florence the balia that condemned him is discovering that the wool trade runs on Medici credit. The diary gives the port, the date, and nothing further.
suggested_refs: Francolino, the Po port of Ferrara, on the fifteenth-century water route to Venice
sources: Janet Ross, Lives of the Early Medici (Gutenberg ebook 74973)

stops.name: Venice, received like an ambassador
stops.date_confidence: Attested; the arrival on 11 October 1433 and the words of the reception are Cosimo's own. The detail of Doge Francesco Foscari's personal patronage during the exile is carried by the dossier and rests on the secondary literature rather than on the diary.
stops.campa: Venice receives a condemned man as a head of state. The Signoria offers him the city and its treasure for his needs, and a house to live in. The Medici have kept a branch here for years and the Venetians know exactly what the Florentine balia has thrown away. Within twelve months the ban will be lifted by the same city that voted it. He is lodged, consulted, and left to write letters, and every letter goes south. He sets down the reception himself: like an ambassador, not like an exile.
stops.quote: like an ambassador, not like an exile
stops.quote_source: Cosimo de' Medici's ricordo of his reception in Venice, in Janet Ross, ed., Lives of the Early Medici (1910), p. 24
suggested_refs: The Doge's Palace under Francesco Foscari and the Medici branch at Venice
sources: Janet Ross, Lives of the Early Medici (Gutenberg ebook 74973)
Research dossier synthesis on Foscari's protection, not independently confirmed

stops.name: Padua, the address the sentence names
stops.date_confidence: Attested; the departure for Padua on 13 October is in Cosimo's own diary. The ten-year sentence assigned Padua, and he later obtained leave to reside anywhere in Venetian territory.
stops.campa: Padua is the address the sentence names, and he goes to it obediently, which is itself a move: he will not be the exile who breaks his terms. The Venetian Signoria repeats its offer to place anything he wants at his disposal. From Padua the bank goes on running, and so does the correspondence with the Florentines who want him back. He takes a house, sends for books, and keeps Michelozzo with him, the architect who followed him out of Florence and who will build for him for the next thirty years.
stops.quote: On the 13th I left for Padua according to command
stops.quote_source: Cosimo de' Medici's ricordo, in Janet Ross, ed., Lives of the Early Medici (1910), p. 25
suggested_refs: Padua under Venetian rule, assigned place of the ten-year exile
sources: Janet Ross, Lives of the Early Medici (Gutenberg ebook 74973)

stops.name: Careggi, the return to his own house
stops.date_confidence: The sources agree on 5 and 6 October 1434 and differ on the sequence. Ross's text has him re-entering Florentine territory on the 5th and reaching Careggi on the 6th; storiadifirenze.org puts him in the city on the 5th and before the pope on the 6th; the Italian record dates the return itself and the start of his ascendancy to 6 October. The conflict is recorded, not resolved. The balia that revoked the ban is dated 28 September by one specialist source and 29 September by others.
stops.campa: Twelve months and eight days after riding out, he crosses back into the Commune at the same point on the road and comes up to the family villa at Careggi for dinner. The house is full of people who have come out to be seen meeting him. Nothing has been fought. He arrives to a meal and not to a triumph. A parliament called in late September voted a new balia and the balia revoked the ban; Rinaldo degli Albizzi and Ridolfo Peruzzi are the men going into exile now.
stops.quote: On the 6th we arrived at our own house, Careggi, to dinner, and found much people.
stops.quote_source: Cosimo de' Medici's ricordo of the return from exile, in Janet Ross, ed., Lives of the Early Medici (1910), p. 27
suggested_refs: The Villa Medici at Careggi, working family property long before its later fame
sources: Janet Ross, Lives of the Early Medici (Gutenberg ebook 74973)
Storia di Firenze, 'Ottobre 1434: Cosimo de' Medici prende il potere'

stops.name: Palazzo dei Priori, the priors and the pope
stops.date_confidence: The palace welcome is dated 5 October by storiadifirenze.org, citing the diary of Pagolo di Matteo Petriboni, and the return itself to 6 October in the Italian record; the papal audience is placed on the day after the palace night. The order of the two days is not settled. The storiadifirenze article could not be retrieved directly and its quotations reach this file at second hand.
stops.campa: He spends a night inside the palace he was arrested in, welcomed by the sitting priors, and the following day Eugenius IV, a pope living in Florence because Rome has thrown him out, receives him and blesses the restoration. Forty-four years later his grandson will stand in the same building and tell the Signoria that Cosimo came back by their unanimous desire. In form that is true. The parliament that voted the recall met in a piazza full of armed men, and the armed men were his. Albizzi and Peruzzi had been condemned four days before he reached the city.
stops.quote: Cosmo, my grandfather, did not return from exile with arms and violence, but by your unanimous desire and approbation.
stops.quote_source: Lorenzo de' Medici to the Florentine Signoria in 1478, reported in Machiavelli, History of Florence, Book VIII (1901 Rennert edition)
suggested_refs: The diary of Pagolo di Matteo Petriboni on the return of October 1434
The condemnation of Rinaldo degli Albizzi and Ridolfo Peruzzi, 2 October 1434
sources: Storia di Firenze, 'Ottobre 1434: Cosimo de' Medici prende il potere'
Machiavelli, History of Florence, archive.org item historyofflorenc00machuoft

stops.name: Palazzo Vecchio, gonfaloniere di giustizia
stops.date_confidence: The first term as gonfalonier falls in the January to February 1435 sitting. The electoral reform through accoppiatori belongs to the balia of 1434 and cannot be assigned a day. Cosimo's claim about banishing no one is his own diary's, and stands against the mass exile the balia had already voted.
stops.campa: For two months he holds the republic's chief magistracy, and his diary records that during his term he banished nobody and commuted death sentences to perpetual imprisonment. The mass exile of his enemies had been voted by the balia before he took office. The real machinery sits elsewhere. Officials called accoppiatori now decide which eligible names go into the leather bags from which magistrates are drawn by lot, and Florence will go on drawing lots for another sixty years. The lot is untouched. The bag is filled in advance.
suggested_refs: The accoppiatori and the borse, the electoral bags of the Florentine republic after 1434
sources: Storia di Firenze, 'Ottobre 1434: Cosimo de' Medici prende il potere'

stops.name: Santa Maria del Fiore, the consecration
stops.date_confidence: Attested: consecrated by Eugenius IV on 25 March 1436, the first day of the year by the Florentine calendar. The research pool tagged this as reconstruction; it is verifiable verbatim and is retagged here.
stops.campa: The dome is closed after sixteen years and Eugenius IV consecrates the cathedral on the first day of the Florentine year. Cosimo is prominent in the negotiations around the ceremony and the indulgences attached to it. He did not pay for the dome. The cathedral works and the wool guild did, and Brunelleschi built it through years when Cosimo held no power at all; that Medici money raised it is a later convenience. The pope comes to the consecration along a raised timber causeway built for him from Santa Maria Novella.
suggested_refs: Brunelleschi's dome, built 1420-1436 for the Opera del Duomo and the Arte della Lana

stops.name: Santa Maria Novella, the emperor in the city
stops.date_confidence: The second term as gonfalonier falls in the January to February 1439 sitting, and the formal reception of the council's participants belongs to it. The council's sessions were held at Santa Maria Novella; the exact building used for the reception itself is not confirmed.
stops.campa: Gonfalonier a second time, he receives the ecumenical council that Medici money has just moved from Ferrara to Florence: John VIII Palaiologos, emperor of a Constantinople with fourteen years left to it, the patriarch Joseph II, Bessarion, and the old Platonist George Gemistos Plethon, who lectures in the city on Plato against Aristotle to men who have read neither in Greek. Union of the Latin and Greek churches is proclaimed in July. In Constantinople it will be repudiated, and the Greek scholars stay in Italy.
suggested_refs: The decree of union Laetentur Caeli, proclaimed at Santa Maria del Fiore on 6 July 1439 and repudiated at Constantinople
The Greek manuscripts and scholars who remained in Italy after the council

stops.name: Palazzo Vecchio, the news from Anghiari
stops.date_confidence: The battle on 29 June 1440 is attested. Cosimo was not present and held no command; this stop stands where he was, in Florence, and not on the field.
stops.campa: Sixty miles east, a Florentine and papal army breaks a Milanese force fighting alongside the exiled Albizzi and their friends, and with it the last armed attempt to undo 1434. Cosimo is not there. He has paid for it, and the exiles who lose the field lose any prospect of ever coming home. Machiavelli, writing seventy years later, will say that one man died in the battle and that he died by falling off his horse, which is a joke about mercenary war and not a casualty return.
suggested_refs: The battlefield of Anghiari, 29 June 1440, and Leonardo da Vinci's lost mural of it painted for the restored republic sixty-four years later

stops.name: Careggi, the death of Lorenzo the Elder
stops.date_confidence: 23 September 1440. The research pool gave 20 September; the dates of Lorenzo di Giovanni de' Medici, 12 October 1394 to 23 September 1440, correct it by three days.
stops.campa: His brother and partner dies at the villa three months after Anghiari, aged forty-five. They have run the bank together since their father's death, gone into exile together, and come home together. Cosimo is now the only senior Medici. Half the house's fortune passes under the hand of a man who does not own it: he takes the guardianship of Lorenzo's son Pierfrancesco and the management of his share of the capital, and he keeps the two shares undivided as long as he can.
suggested_refs: The cadet line of Lorenzo the Elder, the Medici di Pierfrancesco, and the undivided capital of the bank

stops.name: Palazzo Vecchio, the killing of Baldaccio d'Anghiari
stops.date_confidence: The killing on 6 September 1441 is attested. Cosimo's authorization is alleged by contemporaries, Filelfo among them, and repeated by Machiavelli; no surviving order proves it. The contradiction is left standing.
stops.campa: The condottiere Baldaccio d'Anghiari, the best soldier in Florentine pay and the client of Neri Capponi, the one citizen whose standing is comparable to Cosimo's, is summoned to the palace by the gonfalonier Bartolomeo Orlandini. Orlandini's men set on him in an upper room, throw him down into the courtyard, and cut off his head where the crowd can see it. His property is confiscated and his widow is left petitioning. Cosimo gains a rival weakened and says nothing about it in any paper that survives.
suggested_refs: Francesco Filelfo's polemics against Cosimo, and Machiavelli's account of the death of Baldaccio
sources: Research dossier synthesis of Filelfo and Machiavelli, not independently retrieved

stops.name: Bosco ai Frati, the Mugello convent
stops.date_confidence: Attested from 1420, when Cosimo acquired the convent and began financing Michelozzo's rebuilding of the church of San Bonaventura. The research pool tagged this as reconstruction and dated it to the 1440s; both are corrected here, as are coordinates that were 5.5 km out.
stops.campa: In the Mugello, the valley the family came down from, he buys a decayed Franciscan house and puts Michelozzo to rebuilding the church of San Bonaventura. It is the earliest of his religious foundations and it stands thirty miles from the city, in country where the Medici are landlords rather than citizens. The Observant friars get a house. The Medici get a chapel among their own tenants, in the country they would have fallen back on if the road north in 1433 had gone another way. Michelozzo will build for him for the rest of his life.
suggested_refs: The convent of Bosco ai Frati at San Piero a Sieve, rebuilt by Michelozzo from 1420
sources: Italian Wikipedia, 'Convento di Bosco ai Frati'
Dale Kent, Treccani DBI entry on the Mugello holdings

stops.name: Orsanmichele, the guild's Saint Matthew
stops.date_confidence: Cosimo was drawn as a prior of the Arte del Cambio in 1415, which is attested. Ghiberti's bronze Saint Matthew for the guild's niche runs 1419-1422. Cosimo's individual part in the commission is not separately documented; the act is the guild's and not his.
stops.campa: The moneychangers' guild, which drew him as one of its priors five years earlier, casts a bronze Saint Matthew for its niche on the granary church, over life size and larger than anything the rival guilds have put up. Ghiberti takes the contract. A tax collector turned evangelist stands in a stone shell on a public street, paid for by the men who handle other men's money in a city that has never settled whether that is a trade or a sin. Every guild in Florence has a statue on this building.
suggested_refs: Ghiberti's bronze Saint Matthew in the Arte del Cambio niche at Orsanmichele
sources: General guild-patronage history of Orsanmichele, cross-referenced in the research dossier

stops.name: The convent of San Marco
stops.date_confidence: Michelozzo's work at San Marco is dated 1437-1444, with the reference literature giving the project's start as 1437 or 1438 and Fra Angelico resident 1438-1445. The forty thousand florins is the figure given in the literature. The pool's description of a double cell is an overstatement; the source says only that Cosimo kept a cell for his personal retreat.
stops.campa: He takes the convent from one order and hands it to another, then spends some forty thousand florins rebuilding it: cloisters, chapter room, refectory, and sixty cells that Fra Angelico frescoes one by one for men under a vow of poverty. The library goes up to hold Niccolo Niccoli's Greek and Latin manuscripts, bought out of the dead humanist's debts and opened to any scholar who could read them, the first library of its kind in Europe. He keeps a cell in the convent for himself, and goes up to it to be alone.
stops.quote: he sometimes complained to his friends that he had never been able to lay out so much in the service of God as to find the balance in his own favor
stops.quote_source: Machiavelli, History of Florence, Book VII, p. 357 in the 1901 Rennert edition, reporting Cosimo in indirect speech
suggested_refs: Michelozzo's library at San Marco, built for the collection of Niccolo Niccoli
The Medici sculpture garden beside San Marco, where the next generation of the family trained its artists
sources: Visit Tuscany, 'The Museum of San Marco in Florence'
Machiavelli, History of Florence, archive.org item historyofflorenc00machuoft

stops.name: Villa di Cafaggiolo, the Mugello rebuilt
stops.date_confidence: Villegiardinimedicei dates Michelozzo's transformation to 1443-1451; the English reference works date the redesign to 1452. The conflict is recorded and not resolved. The research pool's coordinates were 4.5 km out and are corrected here.
stops.campa: Michelozzo turns the family's old fortified farm into something that is still a fortress: towers, gun ports, a drawbridge, and around it farms, roads, gardens, and fountains laid out for what the humanists are calling doctum otium, learned leisure. The Medici are ten miles from any neighbour who could challenge them here, and the house is built to be held against one anyway. Learned leisure in the Mugello means a library behind a drawbridge. The work is dated 1443 to 1451 in one account and 1452 in another.
suggested_refs: The Villa di Cafaggiolo, remodelled by Michelozzo, now in the UNESCO listing of Medici villas and gardens

stops.name: Palazzo Medici, the house on the Via Larga
stops.date_confidence: The commission to Michelozzo dates to 1444 and building runs to 1484. Vasari's story that Cosimo rejected a more magnificent Brunelleschi design to avoid envy is a later anecdote and not a contemporary record. The quote on envy is reported speech in a 1961 popular history with no primary source traceable behind it.
stops.campa: He builds the family a house on the Via Larga: rusticated stone at the street, a courtyard within, heavy but unbattlemented, a merchant's palace and not a lord's castle. Vasari will tell the story that Brunelleschi offered a grander design, that Cosimo refused it for fear of envy, and that Brunelleschi smashed the model. The building work runs on until 1484, twenty years after Cosimo is dead. In the casa vecchia fifty metres away his grandson Lorenzo de' Medici is born in 1449, into a household whose ledgers are the government of Florence.
stops.quote: there is in gardens a plant which one ought to leave dry, although most people water it. It is the weed called envy
stops.quote_source: Reported speech attributed to Cosimo in Jean Lucas-Dubreton, Daily Life in Florence in the Time of the Medici (1961), p. 58; a twentieth-century popular history with no primary chronicle behind it
suggested_refs: The Palazzo Medici Riccardi on the Via Larga, sold to the Riccardi in 1659 and to the Tuscan state in 1814
Vasari's account in the Lives of the rejected Brunelleschi model
sources: Jean Lucas-Dubreton, Daily Life in Florence in the Time of the Medici (1961), located through the Open Library full-text index

stops.name: Badia Fiesolana, above the city
stops.date_confidence: Attested: the present fabric dates from between 1456 and 1467, when Michelozzo was commissioned by Cosimo for the rebuilding. The research pool tagged this as reconstruction and it is retagged here. The work was unfinished at his death in 1464.
stops.campa: On the hill road to Fiesole he pays for the rebuilding of a canons' house: church, convent, a library, and a cell kept for himself, where he goes to read and is seen going to read. Vespasiano da Bisticci's copyists fill the shelves to order. He is sixty-seven and has taken up the habit his son will not live long enough to inherit, of withdrawing upward out of the city for weeks together. The work is unfinished when he dies in 1464. Five and a half centuries on, the church front is still bare brick.
suggested_refs: The Badia Fiesolana, left unfinished at Cosimo's death, now the seat of the European University Institute

stops.name: Palazzo Medici, the making of a duke of Milan
stops.date_confidence: Sforza entered Milan in 1450 and the Medici loans behind his campaign are attested in Treccani. No single date can be given for the decision to back him, and 1450 orders the segment rather than dating an event.
stops.campa: Filippo Maria Visconti dies without a legitimate son and Milan proclaims itself a republic. Cosimo lends the condottiere Francesco Sforza the money to take it, against the advice of most of the Florentine political class and against seventy years of Florentine policy, which held that Venice was the friend and Milan the enemy. The one man who could pay for a war has chosen which war it will be. Sforza becomes duke on Medici credit, and Florence changes sides. There is no debate and no vote.
suggested_refs: The Medici loans to Francesco Sforza and the reversal of the Florentine-Venetian alliance

stops.name: Palazzo Medici, the letter to Sforza
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction as to the letter itself: its description comes from an auction-house catalogue that returned an error and could not be retrieved. Cosimo's role in the diplomacy before the Peace of Lodi is attested independently in Treccani. The date is new style.
stops.campa: He writes to the duke of Milan about what the pope intends, what Venice and Milan are saying to each other in secret, and which captains can be bought. He holds no office. Six weeks later Milan and Venice make peace at Lodi, Florence joins the settlement that follows, and Italy gets forty years without a general war between its powers. The most important foreign correspondence of the republic is being written in a private study. Whether this particular letter is in his own hand rests on a single auction catalogue that nobody has been able to open.
suggested_refs: The Peace of Lodi, 9 April 1454, and the Italian League that followed it
The autograph or probably autograph letter of 25 February 1454 to Francesco Sforza, described in a Christie's manuscript catalogue
sources: Christie's lot description, cited in the research dossier and inaccessible on attempted retrieval (HTTP 403)

stops.name: Palazzo Vecchio, the catasto and the Hundred
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction. The 1458 restoration of the catasto, the extraordinary balia, and the creation of the Council of One Hundred are reported in the secondary literature consulted but were not verified against a primary source here. Sforza's offer of troops, said to have been refused in 1455, is also unverified tradition.
stops.campa: Popular pressure forces back the catasto, the assessment that taxes a man on what he is actually shown to own, which the regime had allowed to lapse in favour of arrangements kinder to its own supporters. The answer is another parliament, another balia, a fresh scrutiny of the bags, and a Council of One Hundred that the Medici control. Sforza's soldiers under Astorgio Manfredi are in the neighbourhood while it is voted. Three years earlier Cosimo is said to have refused an offer of Milanese troops.
suggested_refs: The Florentine catasto of 1427 and its restoration in 1458
The Council of One Hundred, created by the balia of 1458
sources: Research dossier synthesis citing the George Mason University Catasto project, not independently retrieved

stops.name: Careggi, the Plato manuscripts
stops.date_confidence: Attested: in 1462 Cosimo supplied Marsilio Ficino with Greek manuscripts of Plato and the use of a house near Careggi. The later tradition of a chartered Platonic Academy founded here rests mainly on Ficino's own retrospective texts and is treated by Hankins as a foundation myth; that article was not retrieved directly and the framing is not asserted.
stops.campa: He gives the young Marsilio Ficino a house near the villa and the Greek Plato to work from, and Ficino begins the Latin translation of the whole corpus, which will not be printed until twenty years after Cosimo is dead. What happens at Careggi is patronage and reading: a physician's son translating for an old banker who cannot read the originals. The Platonic Academy, chartered and formal, is a later story told mostly by Ficino, and the memorial volumes written for Cosimo's own death mention no such foundation.
suggested_refs: Ficino's Latin Plato, drafted by 1468-69 and printed in 1484
James Hankins, 'Cosimo de' Medici and the Platonic Academy', Journal of the Warburg and Courtauld Institutes

stops.name: Palazzo Medici, the death of Giovanni
stops.date_confidence: Attested; Giovanni di Cosimo de' Medici died 1 November 1463, and the grandson Cosimino had died in 1459. The remark about too large a house is a traditional anecdote from Vespasiano da Bisticci's life of Cosimo and was not confirmed in the sources retrieved for this file.
stops.campa: His second son dies at forty-two: the able one, who ran the difficult branches and bought the pictures, leaving Piero, gouty and often bedridden, as the heir. Cosimo is seventy-four. The grandson Cosimino had died four years before. What remains of the succession he spent thirty years building toward is one sick man and two boys. Carried through the rooms of the new palace, the old man is remembered saying it was too large a house for so small a family.
suggested_refs: Vespasiano da Bisticci's life of Cosimo, source of the remark on the empty house

stops.name: Careggi, the letters to Bruges
stops.date_confidence: Reconstruction: the July 1464 correspondence with Tommaso Portinari at Bruges is reported in the scholarship on the bank's papers but was not verified against the documents here. The Bruges branch itself was formally founded on 24 March 1439, which is attested.
stops.campa: A month before he dies he is still writing to Bruges, where Tommaso Portinari runs the branch founded in 1439, at the far end of a network that reaches London, Geneva, Avignon, Rome, Venice, Naples, and Milan. The story that his last years were given over to gardens, books, and philosophical conversation is his own preferred version and the humanists' version of him. The ledgers show him managing a branch manager in Flanders from a sickroom in the hills, in July 1464.
suggested_refs: The Bruges branch of the Medici Bank, founded 24 March 1439, and the correspondence of Tommaso Portinari
sources: Research dossier synthesis of Medici bank correspondence scholarship, not independently retrieved

stops.name: Careggi, the death
stops.date_confidence: Attested, 1 August 1464. The joint disease was called gout by contemporaries; a modern skeletal re-reading of the Medici tombs proposes diffuse idiopathic skeletal hyperostosis instead, but the exhumed series is the grand-ducal Medici of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, not Cosimo the Elder, whose remains lie undisturbed in the San Lorenzo crypt. For him the reading rests on the deformed hands in Pontormo's posthumous portrait, not on bone.
stops.campa: He dies at the villa on the first of August, seventy-five years old, after years of a joint disease that had left him carried about the house in a chair. Contemporaries call it gout; his own bones lie undisturbed in the crypt at San Lorenzo and have never been read against the diagnosis. Contessina outlives him; he has outlived his brother, one son, and one grandson. He asks to be buried without pomp. Then Piero opens the books to find out what the family owns, and finds that there is no citizen of consequence in Florence who is not in debt to his father.
stops.quote: His liberality became more obvious after his death, when Piero, his son, wishing to know what he possessed, it appeared there was no citizen of any consequence to whom Cosmo had not lent a large sum of money
stops.quote_source: Machiavelli, History of Florence, Book VII, p. 355 in the 1901 Rennert edition
suggested_refs: Pontormo's posthumous portrait of Cosimo il Vecchio, c. 1518-1519, Uffizi
Tonelli, 'Was it true gout? New interpretations of the skeletal disease(s) of the Medici family', PMC3279076
sources: Machiavelli, History of Florence, archive.org item historyofflorenc00machuoft

stops.name: San Lorenzo, before the high altar
stops.date_confidence: The burial in San Lorenzo before the high altar is attested, as is Verrocchio's floor monument, completed between 1465 and 1467. The exact day of the funeral is not specified in the sources consulted and 2 August orders the sequence.
stops.campa: He asked for no pomp and the city overrode him. They bury him in the crypt in front of the high altar of the church he rebuilt, and within three years a slab of marble and porphyry by Verrocchio marks the place in the pavement above. The day of the funeral itself is not recorded. Every Medici buried in Florence afterward lies arranged around this grave. Donatello, who outlives him by two years, is buried in the same church; the bronze pulpits he left unfinished stand in the nave.
stops.quote: His funeral was conducted with the utmost pomp and solemnity, the whole city following his corpse to the tomb in the church of St. Lorenzo, on which, by public decree, he was inscribed, FATHER OF HIS COUNTRY.
stops.quote_source: Machiavelli, History of Florence, Book VII, 1901 Rennert edition
suggested_refs: Verrocchio's floor monument over the crypt of San Lorenzo, 1465-1467
Donatello's unfinished bronze pulpits in the nave of San Lorenzo
sources: Machiavelli, History of Florence, archive.org item historyofflorenc00machuoft

stops.name: Florence, the title cut into the floor
stops.date_confidence: The decree falls in March 1465, seven months after the death. The title was never held in his lifetime. The research pool described Pater Patriae as an honour last given in antiquity to Cicero; that is wrong, since twenty-three Roman emperors held it after him, and the correct wording is once awarded to Cicero.
stops.campa: Seven months after the funeral the republic decrees by public vote that he be called Pater Patriae, father of the fatherland, and the words are cut into the slab over the crypt. It is a Roman title, awarded once to Cicero and afterward held by twenty-three emperors, and it goes here to a private citizen who never held an office he was not drawn for by lot. He governed for thirty years without a title. The republic granted one in March 1465, and cut it into a floor that people walk on.
stops.quote: He was of middle stature, olive complexion, and venerable aspect; not learned but exceedingly eloquent, endowed with great natural capacity, generous to his friends, kind to the poor, comprehensive in discourse, cautious in advising, and in his speeches and replies, grave and witty.
stops.quote_source: Machiavelli, History of Florence, Book VII, character portrait of Cosimo following the notice of his death, 1901 Rennert edition
suggested_refs: The Pater Patriae inscription on the floor monument at San Lorenzo

Francis Bacon, Apophthegms New and Old no. 206, ascribing to Cosmus, Duke of Florence the saying that we read we ought to forgive our enemies but not that we ought to forgive our friends; the ducal title belonged to Cosimo I, so the attribution to this Cosimo is uncertain
sources: Machiavelli, History of Florence, archive.org item historyofflorenc00machuoft
